transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Camila Ruiz (Redwood SE), Marcus Nguyen (LedgerOak CTO), Sofia Alvarez (LedgerOak SRE), Eliot Park (LedgerOak Product), Nina Rao (LedgerOak QA)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to align POC success criteria, share how the benchmark harness will integrate with LedgerOak's client scripts, and decide streaming vs non-streaming runs and timelines. Discussed telemetry requirements (p95/p99 latency, cold start, KV cache warmup), data handling (redaction, residency), and next steps for artifacts and first benchmark run.

Topics:
- Workload slices (webchat, async batch, peak burst)
- Streaming vs non-streamed inference for their chat UI
- Harness adapter integration and sample scripts
- Success criteria (latency, throughput, cost envelope, quality regression tolerance)
- Timeline and responsibilities

Action items (reiterated in call): see metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE. Camila the SE is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Marcus Nguyen: Good, thanks. Morning for some of us. We'll be brief, we want to get alignment so we can run the first bench.
[00:18] Camila Ruiz: Hi all. Quick agenda — confirm workloads, talk harness hook up, streaming vs non-streamed decisions and then success criteria.
[00:27] Sofia Alvarez: Sounds good. We have a few constraints: SOC2-related audit windows, and we need data redaction rules for PII. Also prefer VPC/private route for the POC if possible.
[00:38] Jordan Lee: Noted. The POC can run on Redwood Dedicated or Private apron — sorry, Private plane? I keep saying weird things — Redwood Private deployment is available; we'll document options but for the benchmark we usually use a hosted sandbox unless you need the VPC immediately.
[00:55] Marcus Nguyen: For this initial run we can use hosted, but the telemetry will need to map to our SRE dashboards. We will also want to validate the VPC flow later.
[01:05] Eliot Park: Quick background: LedgerOak is moving its customer chat and invoice summarization features to an LLM-based pipeline. We want to validate cost/performance numbers before committing to reserved capacity.
[01:17] Camila Ruiz: Great. Can you confirm your expected traffic shapes — do you have both asynchronous batch loads (nightly invoice summarization) and a real-time chat with streaming tokens enabled?
[01:27] Marcus Nguyen: Yes. Three slices: 1) interactive chat — medium QPS, need streaming to avoid perceived latency, 2) nightly batch summarization — large token counts but can be non-streaming, 3) peak burst — sudden spikes when billing runs start. We'll send exact RPS and concurrency numbers.
[01:42] Jordan Lee: Perfect. For the harness we typically ingest client scripts that either call the streaming endpoint or the non-stream streaming generate endpoint. Our adapter can replay their scripts preserving token timing or run synthetic token pacing.
[01:53] Nina Rao: On redaction — we will scrub names, account numbers, and free-text PII before sending. We'll attach our redaction rules. We may want to see logs but with PII masked.
[02:04] Camila Ruiz: We can support masked payloads in the harness and also provide a sample masking step in the adapter.
[02:10] Marcus Nguyen: What metrics will you collect? We need p50/p95/p99, tail cold start, throughput, tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens.
[02:20] Camila Ruiz: Standard telemetry: request timestamps, token counts, pipeline latencies broken down (network, model compute, kv cache lookup when applicable), and custom tags so you can map to your SRE tracing. For cost we provide estimated compute/instance usage and our unit cost model for the POC.
[02:35] Eliot Park: About KV cache — our prompts are heavily prefix-based, so K-V cache warmup matters. How will you model warm vs cold cache?
[02:44] Camila Ruiz: Two approaches: synthetic warmup where we prefill the cache with representative prefix keys, or run a ramp traffic where the harness slowly increases unique prefixes. We'll run both and compare. We log hit rates.
[02:55] Marcus Nguyen: Good. And cold start? We see some vendors with big spikes at cold start. Need p99 there to be bounded.
[03:03] Jordan Lee: We'll include cold-start scenarios in the benchmark: machine scale-up events and new model variant spin-up. We'll capture the tail latency during those events.
[03:13] Sofia Alvarez: For streaming vs non-streaming, our hypothesis is streaming gives better UX but higher cost and complexity. We want to quantify tradeoffs — in particular, end-to-end perceived latency (time to first token) and total tokens consumed.
[03:28] Camila Ruiz: Exactly. Our harness supports both modes in the same script. You can tag a transaction as streaming and the adapter will open an SSE/WebSocket stream, otherwise it will make a single generate call and measure time to full response.
[03:40] Nina Rao: Any known gotchas when integrating with our webchat? We use a client that sends partial messages and sometimes cancels mid-stream.
[03:47] Camila Ruiz: Good call — cancellation scenarios are important. We can simulate mid-stream cancellations and ensure the runtime refunds or truncates token accounting correctly. We'll want your cancel patterns in the sample scripts.
[03:58] Marcus Nguyen: We'll provide those. Also our QA wants a run that mimics heavy jitter and network latencies to validate client-side timeouts.
[04:06] Camila Ruiz: We can decline or inject latency in the harness at the client adapter level to mirror on-prem network conditions.
[04:12] Jordan Lee: Let's walk success criteria draft so we're aligned. Proposed: p95 <= 220 ms for short-chat interactions (time-to-first-token), p99 <= 800 ms, throughput handle 120 rps sustained for the interactive slice, cost target <$2.5 per 1M tokens for the architecture we test, and quality regression WER/semantic drop <5% against your golden set. Thoughts?
[04:36] Eliot Park: The cost target is aggressive but reasonable if we use batching and quantization. Quality thresholds need to be clarified — we'll send a sample eval set and acceptance thresholds.
[04:45] Marcus Nguyen: On p95 220 ms — that sounds tight but feasible if we avoid extra hops. Our infra adds about 50 ms RTT. Can Redwood route within same region for low network hops?
[04:54] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can pin region and we recommend colocated routing for the benchmark. We'll include network latency in the reported breakdown so you can see where those 50 ms are coming from.
[05:04] Sofia Alvarez: For the non-streaming batch job, acceptance is more about cost and throughput: finish nightly jobs within our 2-hour window with <10% cost variance vs estimate.
[05:12] Camila Ruiz: We'll run a scaled batch with concurrency and observe token throughput and autoscaling behavior.
[05:18] Nina Rao: Timeline — when can we expect the bench adapter?
[05:21] Camila Ruiz: I can drop a prototype adapter by Friday, 2027-12-17. It will include a README and sample client script. That matches the timeline you asked for.
[05:29] Jordan Lee: After you share the traffic slices, we'll schedule the initial streaming and non-streaming runs the week of 2027-12-20. We'll aim for two baseline runs (one warm cache, one cold cache) and then targeted stress runs.
[05:40] Marcus Nguyen: How much instrumentation will be visible to us? We want raw event logs and aggregated dashboards.
[05:45] Camila Ruiz: You get both: raw event CSV/ndjson exports and a short-lived dashboard during the POC for quick analysis. We'll also provide a runbook for reproducing the runs.
[05:55] Eliot Park: About security and compliance — we need SOC2 evidence, SSO (SAML), audit logs, and KMS usage for key material if this goes to Private. Any of that available for POC?
[06:06] Jordan Lee: We can provide copies of our security whitepaper, SOC2 attestations, and provide a test SSO integration for the Private deployment. For Hosted sandbox, audit logs are limited but we do show request-level logs with masked fields. Camila, correct me if I'm wrong.
[06:18] Camila Ruiz: Yep. For the sandbox we mask PII; for Private or Dedicated we can configure KMS and enterprise audit retention. We'll attach the security package to the follow-up email.
[06:27] Nina Rao: On data residency — some EU customers require tokens not leave region. Will the POC be region-locked?
[06:33] Jordan Lee: We can run in eu-west or us-east region per your slices. For the POC, pick the region you'd like to validate.
[06:39] Marcus Nguyen: We'll pick us-east for the chat slice and eu-west for the EU testing later. We'll start with us-east.
[06:45] Camila Ruiz: A few technical clarifications for the harness: 1) what client library versions are you using? 2) do you have any custom middleware that rewrites prompts? 3) what's your average prompt length and output token distribution?
[06:57] Marcus Nguyen: We'll export the client call traces and a small sample of prompts (redacted). Client is a Node-based microservice (axios fetch library) with middleware that enriches requests with tenant metadata. Average prompt 120 tokens, expected response 180 tokens for chat; for batch summarization it's more like 2–10k tokens per unit.
[07:15] Camila Ruiz: Huge difference. We'll ensure the harness supports those larger token counts and switch to chunked streaming for the batch runs. For the real-time chat we'll keep streaming per-token.
[07:24] Jordan Lee: On autoscaling and resource sizing — do you have a target budget or are we exploring cost curves?
[07:30] Marcus Nguyen: Both. We want a sizing recommendation for steady-state and an estimate for reserved capacity pricing vs on-demand. So the experiment should capture unit economics across load.
[07:40] Camila Ruiz: We'll include recommended GPU types and instance counts based on observed throughput during the POC and provide a cost model comparing on-demand vs reserved.
[07:48] Sofia Alvarez: Any constraints on the harness side about running long batch jobs? We sometimes push thousands of long sequences; can the harness keep connections stable?
[07:57] Camila Ruiz: Harness supports chunked uploads and heartbeats to keep sessions alive; for extremely long sequences we recommend chunking and streaming the chunks. We'll test long seqs in a separate long-duration run.
[08:07] Marcus Nguyen: Ok. Let's confirm success criteria concretely so there's no ambiguity: we'll deliver the eval set, you'll deliver the benchmark report with raw logs, dashboard, and sizing recommendations, and then we sign off if thresholds met.
[08:20] Jordan Lee: I'll send a success criteria template tonight. Can you fill in the thresholds for quality, latency, and cost by 2027-12-16?
[08:27] Marcus Nguyen: Yes.
[08:28] Camila Ruiz: A couple of gotchas I want to call out from other POCs: 1) mismatched token accounting between client and runtime — we'll include a token reconciliation step, 2) streaming cancellation accounting, and 3) KV cache warmup variance. We'll instrument counters for those.
[08:43] Nina Rao: Good to know. Also, we want to test failure injections — abrupt node restarts — to validate graceful degradation.
[08:50] Camila Ruiz: We'll perform controlled failure injection during a stress run and capture fallback behavior.
[08:55] Jordan Lee: Last part, logistics: Camila will send the adapter on 12/17. Marcus and team send traffic slices and redaction rules by 12/16. We'll book two 2-hour windows for the benchmark week of 12/20; Jordan will propose times in follow-up.
[09:10] Marcus Nguyen: That works. Any docs to attach?
[09:13] Jordan Lee: I'll attach our POC runbook, sample harness adapter, and security package. Camila will add the adapter repo.
[09:20] Eliot Park: Quick question — do you support client-side mirroring so we can run the harness against a copy of live traffic in a dry-run mode?
[09:28] Camila Ruiz: Yes, traffic mirroring is supported with transforms and masking; we'll need to set that up with your infra team for a safe dry-run.
[09:35] Marcus Nguyen: We'll follow up on that separately.
[09:38] Jordan Lee: Great. If there are no more questions we'll wrap. Thanks everyone. Camila, over to you for next emails.
[09:45] Camila Ruiz: I'll send the adapter and README, plus a checklist for the traffic slices. Expect that by Friday.
[09:51] Nina Rao: Thanks all.
[09:53] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: ASR mis-transcribed some product names intermittently ("Redwood Dedicatedness", "K-V cash"), and speaker overlap caused a few attributions to be generic. The content has been lightly cleaned for legibility but retains filler language and partial words.
